text: ← Foundations contents THE LEARNING PATH WHAT YOU WILL LEARNDistinguish natural and thermal broadening and calculate temperature scaling. 01First define the width We use the full width at half maximum (FWHM): the full separation between the two half-height points. Standard deviations and half-widths have different numerical factors; always specify the convention. 02Finite lifetimes produce natural broadening A wave lasting only a finite time has a spread of frequencies, unlike an endless monochromatic wave. A shorter excited-state lifetime gives a broader natural line. We use the following result from wave analysis. Δνnat,FWHM = 12πτ For a long-lived lower level and negligible additional broadening. The natural profile is Lorentzian. The estimate ΔEΔt ≈ ℏ does not fix the FWHM coefficient. The exact profile convention matters. 03Atoms move toward and away from us Δνν0 ≈ vlosc, σv = √(kBTm) vlos is positive toward the observer; σv is the one-dimensional velocity standard deviation. We assume |v| ≪ c. Δνth,FWHM = ν0c√(8 ln 2 · kBTm) A Gaussian distribution of line-of-sight thermal velocities gives a Gaussian frequency profile. Its FWHM is 2√(2 ln 2) ≈ 2.355 times the standard deviation. 04Compare the widths for hydrogen at 10,000 K Hydrogen has σᵥ ≈ 9.1 km/s and a thermal FWHM of about 21 km/s. At Lyα, ν₀ ≈ 2.47 × 10¹⁵ Hz, so Δνth ≈ 1.8 × 10¹¹ Hz. A 2p lifetime of about 1.6 ns gives a natural width near 1.0 × 10⁸ Hz. Thermal broadening dominates the core in this example, but Lorentzian wings decline slowly and can still matter far from line centre. Combining the two gives a Voigt profile. Collisions, turbulence, rotation, and instruments can add further broadening. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. If the temperature of hydrogen gas quadruples, what happens to its thermal line width? Show the answer and reasoning It doubles: thermal width scales as √(T/m). At the same temperature, heavier atoms have narrower thermal lines. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS These sources support the laws and numerical values; some use university-level mathematics.
